title: Out of Gas: New York’s Blocked Pipelines Will Hurt Northeast Consumers
summary: A 2019 Manhattan Institute report argues blocked gas pipelines raise Northeast energy costs and that heat pumps are a poor substitute for gas heating.

assertions.quote: But heat pumps are not efficient in regions where temperatures fall near or below freezing on a regular basis.

verdicts.note: Modern heat pumps keep seasonal COPs around 2 or higher in cold climates; the claim reflects older units.
Cold-climate units listed by NEEP keep COP of 2 or more at 5F, well below freezing, and the modelled cold-climate unit keeps 85% capacity at 5F.
For minimum-efficiency units, cold-climate cities see peak demand more than double at full adoption because the heat pump must regularly run at very low temperatures, which lowers performance.
RMI's cold-climate unit still has a COP of 2.1 at 17F, twice as efficient as resistance heat, even though efficiency drops from 3.5 at 47F.
Edwards' NEEP-based fit (COP = 0.05T + 1.6) gives a COP of about 3.2 at 32F; only single-stage units below 5F are assumed to fall to resistance-level efficiency.
In Minnesota, where winter is mostly below freezing, cold-climate heat pumps kept system efficiencies high and cut heating costs 30-56% against propane and resistance baselines.

Measured COPs stayed above 1.0 at nearly all temperatures in a climate where half of winter hours were below 30-38 F, so units were efficient in energy terms; they were still uneconomic against gas at those prices.
Median field COPs were 1.6-2.7 across all bins below 30 F, about double resistance heat, although total system COP with auxiliary heat was lower in the coldest bins.
Modern standard heat pumps perform well down to -8 to -10°C, well below freezing, and cold-climate units to -25°C (secondary citations).
In Maine, where winter temperatures are often well below freezing, 166 metered units averaged a seasonal heating COP of 3.15 including defrost, and 2 even at -10F.
